sullen

/SUL-en/ — rhymes with pollen · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sullen describes someone who is silently irritable or gloomy, often sulking instead of speaking up.

The sullen teenager stared out the window and answered in one-word grunts.

Example

After the argument, the sullen student withdrew into their own corner, neither engaging with the others nor explaining their anger, just staring with dark eyes and giving short, curt responses.

This is not just irritability—it's the specific combination of being irritable and silent, and sulking. Sullen names this exact behavior: inward withdrawal and moody silence alongside irritation. Plain 'anger' wouldn't capture the silent, brooding quality.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

moody: Moody means prone to mood swings — cheerful one hour, gloomy the next, with little warning. It is about changeability over time. Sullen names one fixed, heavy state: gloomy, irritable silence that settles in and stays. A moody person cycles up and down; a sullen person broods in place.

sulky: Sulky means silently cross about one specific disappointment — not getting your way, losing a game — and it usually passes once the moment does. Sullen is heavier and longer-lasting: a settled habit of gloomy, irritable silence that needs no fresh excuse. A sulky mood blows over; a sullen one lingers.

brooding: Brooding means silently turning dark or unhappy thoughts over and over in your mind — it describes what is happening inside someone's head. Sullen describes what everyone else can see: the gloomy face, the one-word answers, the irritable silence. A brooding person is lost in thought; a sullen person shows the bad mood.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cheerful: visibly happy and in good spirits

upbeat: positive and lively in attitude

Where it sits · how much bad temper fills the silence — quiet → withdrawn → grumpy → sullen

quiet vs. sullen: Quiet just means not talking much, but sullen adds a dark, resentful mood to the silence.

withdrawn vs. sullen: Withdrawn describes pulling away from others; sullen goes further, adding gloomy irritation to that distance.

grumpy vs. sullen: Grumpy means openly bad-tempered, while sullen is stronger, mixing that ill temper with brooding silence.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sullen

Root — sullen: originally 'solitary, alone,' from Latin solus — it drifted through Old French and Middle English solein to 'gloomy from keeping to oneself'

Put it together

Put it together: Sullen traces back through Middle English solein to Latin solus, 'alone' — someone sullen acts alone even in company, withdrawing into gloomy, irritable silence. The root is fossilized: you can no longer see 'alone' in the modern spelling.

Use the root in a new word: sullenness

Use the root in a new word: sullenness: His sullenness after the game made the whole car ride home feel heavy.

Word Building

Word Choice

neutral

Sullen is more specific than 'moody'—it implies not just changeability but a particular kind of stubborn gloominess mixed with irritability. Use sullen when someone is noticeably withdrawn, gloomy, and irritable all at once.
